UK Pushes for Global Levies on Polluting Industries

What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,…

The UK is leading a drive to have countries consider small levies on polluting industries globally to raise funding for climate initiatives in developing countries, which are the worst affected by climate change.

The UK plans to continue pushing for a conversation about levies on polluting sectors into 2027, when it will be the president of the G-20 group of nations.

This week, a declaration at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya is expected to acknowledge the idea of “small levies” to raise climate funding, Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday, citing a draft document it has seen.

“We recognize the potential of innovative approaches to complement existing sources of public and private finance,” the declaration reads.

The document also calls for moving from “repeated and incremental crisis response to one of sustained and transformational resilience-building and proactive financing to match the scale of this challenge.”

At the start of the COP31 summit in Turkey last week, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that a fossil fuel windfall tax can help pay for the energy transition.

“Taxing fossil fuel windfalls can help pay for all this – and shield families from the next price shock,” Guterres said in his remarks at COP 31.

Meanwhile, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said at COP31 that the UK would aim to show leadership in global climate issues that have taken a backseat in recent years, as Britain remains committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and working with all its partners to reach their respective climate goals.

“Britain will live up to its commitments. We will help our friends as they live up to theirs. Britain is back and ready to play its full part,” Burnham said.

The Antalya summit, however, faces difficult negotiations until Friday, when it is scheduled to end, with even the electrification pledge priority of the host country, Turkey, in peril.

The summit may end without a pledge to boost electrification as major developing countries have signaled they would not support a firm commitment, anonymous sources with knowledge of the private talks told Bloomberg on Monday.
